Newly hatched Florida lancelets emerge from fertilised ova at a total length of approximately 0.3 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.3 centimeters], a diminutive size that reflects the minimal yolk reserves allocated to the embryo during its brief incubation. This early developmental stage is completed rapidly; under stable thermal conditions at 30.5 °C [T = 30.5 °C], hatching occurs after roughly 2.5 days [ab = roughly 2.5 days], an interval that aligns with the accelerated developmental rates typical of subtropical lancelet populations. The corresponding wet weight at this neonate stage is remarkably low, calculated at about 0.000072 grams [Wwb = about 0.000072 grams], a value that underscores the extreme altriciality of the newly hatched larva. Such a modest initial mass imposes a critical reliance on exogenous feeding almost immediately after hatching, as endogenous energy reserves are insufficient to sustain prolonged planktonic existence. The combination of a small body size and a brief embryonic period represents an adaptive strategy common among cephalochordates inhabiting warm, productive coastal waters, where rapid initiation of feeding offsets the vulnerability associated with a diminutive starting point.

As the planktonic larva develops, a pivotal morphogenetic event—larval metamorphosis—marks the transition from a free-swimming ichthyoplankton to a benthic juvenile. At this juncture, the organism attains a total length of approximately 0.5 centimeters , a measurement that signals the commencement of body plan reorganisation characteristic of the post-larval transformation. The age at which this milestone occurs is strongly dependent upon ambient temperature; at a cooler regime of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], metamorphosis requires roughly 45 days  to complete, reflecting a decelerated metabolic pace. In contrast, under warmer conditions typical of summer shoals, at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the same developmental transition is accomplished in only 28 days , illustrating the pronounced thermal sensitivity of somatic differentiation in this species. The wet weight of the newly metamorphosed juvenile at this stage is approximately 0.000317 grams , a mass that represents a more than fourfold increase over the larval starting weight and signifies the accumulation of somatic tissue during the pelagic feeding phase.

Sexual maturation in the Florida lancelet is attained following a period of juvenile growth during which the individual undergoes considerable increases in both length and mass. The total length at puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal activity, has been recorded at roughly 2.3 centimeters [Lp = roughly 2.3 centimeters], a size that is typically reached several weeks after settlement. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 0.026 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.026 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment that precedes reproductive activation. First reproduction, marking the initiation of gamete release, occurs after a specific developmental interval: under the standard laboratory temperature of 30.5 °C [T = 30.5 °C], the age at first spawning is approximately 42 days [tR = approximately 42 days]. This relatively short interval to first reproduction, when compared to other marine invertebrates of similar body size, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises early reproductive output in a seasonally productive environment. The attainment of sexual maturity thus represents a critical life-history switch, after which energy is partitioned between continued somatic growth and gamete production.

The maximum documented reproductive output of the Florida lancelet highlights the species capacity for substantial fecundity. During a single spawning event, females release between 1000 and 5000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 1000 and 5000 eggs per spawning event], a broad range that likely reflects individual variation in body condition and resource availability. Multiple spawning events occur over the breeding season; on average, females release 3000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3000 eggs per clutch] and spawn approximately once every 12 days [F_R_i = spawn approximately once every 12 days], resulting in a high cumulative reproductive output under stable laboratory conditions at 30.5 °C [T = 30.5 °C]. The ultimate total length attained by adults is approximately 6.0 centimeters [Li = approximately 6.0 centimeters], a value derived from measurements of the congener Branchiostoma belcheri that provides a useful comparative benchmark for assessing the growth potential of Branchiostoma floridae under optimal conditions.

The maximum lifespan documented for the Florida lancelet reaches approximately 2008 days [am = approximately 2008 days] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 30.5 °C [T = 30.5 °C]. This extended longevity, which exceeds the lifespan of many comparably sized marine invertebrates, allows for repeated reproductive cycles across multiple breeding seasons. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum adult body size approaches 0.4218 grams [Wwi = 0.4218 grams], a value that reflects the accumulation of gonadal and somatic tissues over the organism lifetime. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of sexual maturity as energetic resources are increasingly directed toward gametogenesis. The combination of a moderately extended lifespan and iteroparous reproduction positions Branchiostoma floridae as a species capable of sustained population maintenance through repeated spawning bouts. Comparative studies with other members of the family Branchiostomidae suggest that this life-history pattern, characterised by early maturity, high fecundity, and moderate longevity, is well suited to the relatively stable but food-limited conditions of shallow, subtidal sand flats.
